# How Hoori found its canonical form

The ASCII form *hoori* is not missing anything that ​this name requires. **Hoori** is the canonical spelling supported by the Japanese characters evidence and the tradition's scholarly conventions. This post explains what that form preserves, how it is pronounced, which narratives ‌surround it, and why consistency matters. There are no recovered accents to celebrate; there is something more useful — a spelling whose history can actually be checked.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** ‌Hoori
- **ASCII form:** hoori
- **Meaning:** "Fire-subduing"
- **Domain of influence:** Agriculture, Hunter
- **Pantheon:** Japanese
- **Restoration:** ASCII-equivalent form
- **Original script:** 火折命 (Japanese characters)

## Overview

**Hoori** (*hoori*) — Agriculture, Hunter · Fire-subduing — belongs to ​the Japanese tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Agriculture, Hunter". The name means "Fire-subduing".

**Hoori** is the younger son of Ninigi and Konohana-Sakuya-hime, the husband of the sea princess Toyotama, ​and the great-grandfather of Japan's first emperor, Jimmu. His name, 'Fire-Subduing,' marks him as the brother who overcame Hoderi's fire and whose line would rule the land.

PuniCodex records the canonical scholarly ​spelling **Hoori** and serves its temple at [its temple](https://punicodex.com/hoori/). The displayed form is ASCII-equivalent — a description computed from the displayed form itself. The plain ASCII form *hoori* contains the same letters: ​no recovered diacritics or special encoding is claimed. The work here is consistent citation, capitalization, provenance, and cultural context.

## The Name

The name is attested in Japanese characters as **火折命**. Etymologically it ​means "Fire-subduing".

The canonical spelling **Hoori** matches the conventional scholarly romanization. The plain ASCII form *hoori* contains the same letters, so no lost diacritics or encoding transition is claimed. The editorial work ‌is to fix one reviewed reference spelling, preserve capitalization and provenance, and keep the original evidence visible. The displayed form is ASCII-equivalent — a description computed from the displayed form itself.

The ​letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **h** → **H** — Same, capitalized
- **o** → **o** — Same
- **o** → **o** — Same
- **r** → **r** — Same
- **i** → **i** — Same

## The Original Script

​The name is written in Japanese characters as **火折命**. That attested script remains the primary evidence for the conventional romanization **Hoori**. The canonical Latin spelling does not pretend to recover marks it ‌never contained: it fixes one reviewed reference form while leaving the original script visible for comparison.

The Kojiki writes his name 火折命, Hoori-no-mikoto, conventionally glossed 'Fire-Subduing Lord': 火 'fire' + 折 'to ​break, subdue' + 命, the honorific for a kami. The same prince bears the fuller name 彦火火出見尊, Hikohohodemi-no-mikoto. His brother is 火照命 Hoderi-no-mikoto, 'Fire-Shining Lord' — one word burns steady, the other ‌breaks what burns.

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/hoː.ɾi/** — Modern Standard Japanese (Hepburn).

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **Hō-** — Voiceless glottal [h] plus long open-mid back [oː]; from 火 ​'fire'
- **-ri** — Alveolar tap [ɾ] plus close front [i]; from 折 'to subdue/break'

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: 'HOH-ree' — hold the first syllable long; the 'r' ‌is a light tap.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Japanese** — 火折命 (Hoori-no-mikoto), 'Fire-Subduing Lord' (Kojiki); also 彦火火出見尊 Hikohohodemi-no-mikoto
- **Brother** — Hoderi (火照命, Fire-Shining Lord), his elder brother, master of ​the sea's fortune
- **Descendant** — Great-grandfather of Emperor Jimmu through his son Ugayafukiaezu (Kojiki I; Nihon Shoki I)

Hoori is a plain restoration in this restoration: the long ō is not represented, ​so the ASCII form is identical to Hepburn. He is a pivotal ancestor in the imperial genealogy.

## Mythology

Hoori's mythology is the bridge between the heavenly descent of Ninigi and the earthly ​reign of Emperor Jimmu: a story of exchanged tools, a lost hook, a voyage to the dragon palace, a broken promise, and a line of kings. It is told in the Kojiki ​and repeated, with variations, in the Nihon Shoki.

### The Exchanged Tools (Kojiki)

The youngest son of Ninigi and Konohana-Sakuya-hime received from his father the **bow**, while his elder brother Hoderi received the ​**fishhook** — one son of the mountains, one of the sea, mirroring the division of the land itself (Kojiki I). Hoori proposed that they exchange tools for a single day: he would ‌try his brother's fortune with the hook, Hoderi the mountains with the bow. The day went well for no one. Hoori, inexpert at the shore, lost the borrowed hook in the sea, ​and when he dived and dragged the bottom it could not be found. Hoderi refused every substitute — first his own sword, then five hundred mother-of-pearl hooks, then a thousand — demanding ‌back the one original hook, the single object through which a man's fortune was thought to run. The impossible demand drives the younger brother out of the human world and down into ​the sea: the quarrel over one small thing is what opens the door to the gods.

### The Dragon Palace of Watasumi (Kojiki)

Following the counsel of an old man on the beach ‌— one of the passing kami who advise heroes at their lowest hour — Hoori sat on the bough of a tree that bent over the waves until the tide carried him ​down through a gateway into the undersea palace of **Watasumi-no-kami**, the sea deity. There he was welcomed, bathed, feasted, and married to the sea god's daughter **Toyotama-hime**, the 'Abundant-Jewel Princess' (Kojiki I). ‌When Hoori confessed why he had come, Toyotama's brother searched the sea and recovered the lost hook from the throat of a red sea-bream. Watasumi then gave his son-in-law two treasures — ​the tide-flowing jewel and the tide-ebbing jewel, with which any sea can be raised or stilled — and taught him the ruse by which a proud man is broken: do not ‌answer rage with rage, but **mock it gently as it rages**, and its strength will spend itself against your calm. The palace gives the exiled brother everything his own shore withheld: a ​wife, the hook, and a strategy.

### The Mocked Brother and the Covenant (Kojiki)

Hoori returned to land and waited on the beach. When Hoderi came raging across the strand, Hoori sang a ​mocking song — as the Kojiki has it, like the bushes on the shore his brother's beard was tangled, like the drifting seaweed his rage floated aimlessly — and Hoderi attacked. Hoori ‌raised the tide-flowing jewel, and the sea rose to Hoderi's neck; Hoderi begged and wept, and Hoori raised the ebbing jewel and spared him (Kojiki I). The brothers made peace on a ‌new order: Hoderi would keep the watery ways, and his descendants would serve Hoori's line forever. Thus the sea-fortune and the mountain-fortune were divided as they still are in Japan — and ‌the humbler brother, who had lost everything in the water, came home owning both the land and the sea's obedience. The myth's arithmetic is deliberate: the borrowed hook cost nothing to replace, ​but the brotherly covenant it purchased was the real prize.

### The Broken Taboo and the First Emperor (Kojiki)

Toyotama came up from the sea to bear her child, but first she built ​a parturition hut roofed with cormorant feathers and laid down the law that Hoori must not look inside. Curiosity — the flaw and the engine of this whole cycle — overcame him. ‌He peeked and saw his wife in her true shape, a great **sea-dragon** coiled in the hut; mortified, Toyotama abandoned the land and the newborn, sending her sister **Tamayori-hime** in her place ​with a parting song. The child, **Ugayafukiaezu**, was raised by his aunt, married her in time, and their son was Kamuyamato-Iwarebiko — better known as **Emperor Jimmu**, first emperor of Japan (Kojiki ​I; Nihon Shoki I). Hoori's one act of disobedience costs him his wife, yet it leaves the imperial line on land, guarded by sea and mountain at once. The sources read the ‌episode without apology: the line of emperors begins exactly where the promise was broken.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography associated with Hoori concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a ​compressed statement about the name:

- **Bow** — The weapon Ninigi gave him, symbolizing rule over the mountains
- **Fishhook** — The lost and recovered hook that brought his brother Hoderi to submission
- **Sea ​palace (Ryūgū)** — The undersea realm where he won Toyotama
- **Cormorant feather robe** — The gift that allowed him to travel between land and sea

- **Bow** — The weapon Ninigi gave him, ‌symbolizing rule over the mountains

## Archaeology & Evidence

Hoori has no shrine and no image, but his story is anchored in real ground. The Kojiki and Nihon Shoki place the action ​in the Yamato basin: Jimmu's traditional tomb, the Unebi kofun, lies by Kashihara in Nara Prefecture, and **Kashihara Jingū** — founded in 1890 — marks the traditional site of Kashihara-no-miya, the palace ‌from which Jimmu set out eastward. His narrative survives materially in the **Shinpukuji-bon**, the early thirteenth-century manuscript of the Kojiki kept at Shinpuku-ji in Nagoya, the sole complete copy of the lost ​712 original. At the foot of Mount Miwa, the Ōmiwa shrine preserves the sacred landscape in which the Jimmu-cycle myths were first localized. The evidence is commemorative rather than contemporary — but ​for an eighth-century state charter, that is precisely the point.

## Realm & Domain

**Hoori** is the younger son of Ninigi and Konohana-Sakuya-hime, the husband of the sea princess Toyotama, and the great-grandfather ​of Japan's first emperor, Jimmu. His name, 'Fire-Subduing,' marks him as the brother who overcame Hoderi's fire and whose line would rule the land.

### Master of the Mountains

He received the bow ​and became a hunter of the highlands.

### Husband of Toyotama

Married the daughter of the sea god Ryūjin in the undersea palace.

### Father of Ugayafukiaezu

His son by Toyotama continued the line ‌to Emperor Jimmu.

### Imperial Forebear

His story explains how the imperial line gained legitimacy from both sea and land.

## Across Cultures

Hoori's story fuses motifs common across East Asia: the mortal who ‌journeys to the dragon palace (parallels in Chinese and Korean legend), the animal bride whose true form must never be seen, and the younger brother whose misfortune ripens into sovereignty. Within Japan ​the dragon-palace voyage lived on most famously in the folktale of **Urashima Tarō**, where the same palace, the same time-slip, and the same broken promise end far more cruelly. Buddhist Japan had ‌no need to give Hoori an avatar — his tale was too useful to the state to remain folklore. Written into the Kojiki (712) and Nihon Shoki (720), it became the founding ​charter of the imperial house, read at court and cited by every dynasty that traced itself to Jimmu. The motifs are pan-Asian; the genealogy is specifically Yamato.

Kindred figures in the PuniCodex ​cross-tradition index include [[hoderi|Hoderi]] (elder and younger fire brothers), [[toyotama|Toyotama]] (hunter husband and sea wife), [[ugayafukiaezu|Ugayafukiaezu]] (father and ancestor of Jimmu), [[anahita|Anāhitā]] (earth / mother / fertility), [[anat|ꜥAnat]] (hunt / wild), and ‌[[artemis|Ártemis]] (hunt / wild).

## Cultural Legacy

Hoori is remembered almost entirely as an ancestor, but his story has never stopped being retold. The dragon palace resurfaces in Heian tales, in *otogizōshi* storybooks, ‌in puppet-theatre and Kabuki adaptations, and in modern novels, manga, and anime — the sea-bride and the undersea court are among Japan's most durable images. Politically his line still matters: the traditional ‌date of Jimmu's accession, the first day of the first month of 660 BCE, became *Kigensetsu* in 1872 and survives as National Foundation Day (11 February). The imperial regalia — mirror, ‌sword, and jewel — descend through this very genealogy, so that Hoori's tide-jewels and his descendants' legitimacy remain, ritually, in the same family.

The account of Hoori given in ​this edition rests on the witnesses and reference works listed below. Lexica and etymological dictionaries secure the form and meaning of the name; the literary and religious texts supply the narrative evidence.

## A Meditation

Hoori is the one who looked. His whole career turns on ​small acts with enormous consequences: he borrows a hook and loses an empire's worth of trouble; he accepts a bride and gains the sea; he peeks through a feathered wall and loses ​her — and founds a dynasty. The Kojiki does not condemn him. Instead it makes curiosity the very mechanism by which the imperial line comes to land: no broken taboo, no Jimmu. ​It is a strikingly unsentimental theology of legitimacy, closer to a political founding document than a moral tale: the state begins not in obedience but in transgression survived. Hoori also teaches a ‌subtler lesson about rivalry. He never defeats his brother by force; he wins by patience, by the tide-jewels, and by a mocking song. The victor in this myth is the one who ​can wait on the beach while his brother's rage exhausts itself against the sea.

The original evidence — **火折命** in Japanese characters — carries semantic and phonetic information that no romanization ​can fully reproduce.

By fixing one reviewed spelling as the public reference, the project prevents the drift that occurs when a name is romanized differently in every article, map, and database. The ‌character list shows exactly what is carried forward. "No change" here means a deliberate choice to keep the name stable, searchable, and faithful to the record.
